lines.text: Last time ended with one step still done by hand: someone running kubectl apply from their laptop.
lines.say: Last time ended with one step still done by hand: someone running cube control apply from their laptop.

lines.text: Today a controller takes that job, and Git becomes the one place that says what should be running.

scenes.title: What goes wrong with apply by hand

boxes.label: who applied this, and from which copy of the files?
a quick fix made in the cluster, never put back in Git
does the cluster match main right now? nobody can say
and everyone who deploys needs write access to prod

lines.text: Applying by hand works, and it's how we've built everything so far. But it pushes from wherever someone happens to be.
Was that applied from main, or from a branch that never merged? The cluster can't tell you.
Someone fixes something in a hurry, straight in the cluster, and the fix never makes it back to Git. The next apply quietly undoes it.
After a few months, nobody can say for sure whether prod matches what's in the repo.
And everyone who deploys needs write access to the production cluster.

scenes.title: The reconcile loop, one level up

boxes.label: Episode 0: desired state, actual state, and a controller closing the gap
it pulls from Git: nobody outside needs to reach the cluster
it runs inside the cluster, as pods, like everything else

lines.text: Argo CD flips it around. Its desired state is a folder in a Git repository: for us, the prod overlay from last time.
It reads that folder, compares it with what's in the cluster, and applies the difference.
That's the reconcile loop from Episode 0. A Deployment controller keeps pods matching a Deployment. Argo CD keeps the whole cluster matching Git.
And it pulls. Nothing outside the cluster pushes to it, so no laptop or pipeline needs prod credentials.
Argo CD itself is just more pods, in its own namespace, installed like everything else.
We install it the way we installed Loki and cert-manager: a HelmChart resource, which k3s' Helm controller turns into a release, in the argocd namespace.
lines.say: We install it the way we installed Loki and cert-manager: a Helm Chart resource, which K three S's Helm controller turns into a release, in the Argo C D namespace.

lines.text: A few values. Plain names for the parts, so the pods are called argocd-server and so on, without the release name in front.
lines.say: A few values. Plain names for the parts, so the pods are called Argo C D server and so on, without the release name in front.

lines.text: Argo CD has a web UI with its own sign-in, which could go through Keycloak. We'll use the command line instead, so the bundled sign-in service is off.
And the company's root certificate from Episode 9, so Argo CD trusts git.corp.internal when it fetches the repo over HTTPS.
Apply it, and k3s starts the install.
lines.say: Apply it, and K three S starts the install.

lines.text: A minute and a half later, six pods. Two matter most today.
The repo server fetches the repository and renders it, running Kustomize for us.
The application controller is the loop itself: it compares what the repo server rendered with the cluster, and applies the difference.
Argo CD adds a new kind of object: an Application. It tells Argo CD what to watch, and where to put it.
The source: our repository on the company's Git server, the main branch, and the prod overlay.
The destination: this same cluster, in the golinks namespace.
lines.say: The destination: this same cluster, in the go links namespace.

lines.text: Then the sync policy. Automated means Argo CD applies changes itself, instead of waiting for someone to press a button.
Prune means a file deleted from Git gets its object deleted from the cluster too.
And self heal means a change made straight in the cluster gets put back. A second Application does the same for dev, from the dev overlay.

scenes.title: What Argo CD needs to reach Git

boxes.label: a read-only token, in a Secret made by hand: never in Git
the company root CA, from the chart's values, to trust its HTTPS
read access is all it needs: it never writes to the repo

lines.text: The repository is private, so Argo CD needs a way in.
A read-only token from the Git server goes in a Secret, labeled so Argo CD finds it. Like the Postgres password, it's made by hand and never committed.
The CA certificate we already saw lets it check the server's HTTPS.
Read access is enough. Argo CD never writes to the repository; people do, through pull requests.
This is the last kubectl apply for golinks. Two Applications, one for each environment.
lines.say: This is the last cube control apply for go links. Two Applications, one for each environment.

lines.text: Both read as synced and healthy. Everything was already running, so Argo CD compared, found it all matching, and simply took over.
Synced means the cluster matches Git. Healthy means the objects themselves are fine: pods ready, Deployments rolled out.

steps.command: argocd app get golinks | grep -E '^(Name|- Repo|  Path|Sync|Health)'

lines.text: For more detail, there's the argocd command line. In core mode it uses kubectl's own access, so the namespace has to point at argocd first.
lines.say: For more detail, there's the Argo C D command line. In core mode it uses cube control's own access, so the namespace has to point at Argo C D first.

lines.text: Log in with the core flag. No password: it talks straight to the cluster's API.
argocd app get shows one Application. Here filtered to the useful lines.
lines.say: Argo C D app get shows one Application. Here filtered to the useful lines.

lines.text: The repo and the path, the automated policy, and the exact commit the cluster matches right now. That's the question nobody could answer before.

steps.command: kubectl patch cm golinks-config -n golinks -p '{data: {LOG_LEVEL: debug}}'
kubectl get cm golinks-config -n golinks -o jsonpath='{..LOG_LEVEL}'; echo

lines.text: Now the drift test. Someone turns on debug logging in prod, straight in the cluster, with kubectl patch.
lines.say: Now the drift test. Someone turns on debug logging in prod, straight in the cluster, with cube control patch.

lines.text: Watch the Application. Argo CD watches the objects it manages, so it sees the change at once, and marks the app out of sync.
Self heal kicks in, and a few seconds later it's synced again.
LOG_LEVEL is back to info, as Git says. The running pods read their config at start, so they never even saw the change.
lines.say: Log level is back to info, as Git says. The running pods read their config at start, so they never even saw the change.

lines.text: To really turn on debug logging in prod, change the overlay and open a pull request. That's the point.

scenes.title: Argo CD only guards what Git says

boxes.label: a field Git doesn't set is left to whoever owns it

lines.text: A second test teaches something. Someone scales golinks down to one pod by hand.
lines.say: A second test teaches something. Someone scales go links down to one pod by hand.

lines.text: Remember Episode 11: the Deployment in Git has no replicas field, because the HPA owns the count.
So Argo CD has nothing to compare. The app stays synced, and Argo CD leaves it alone.
The HPA puts it back instead, to at least two pods, within a few seconds.
That's the rule. Argo CD only guards the fields that Git sets, and anything Git leaves out belongs to someone else, which is exactly what we want here.

boxes.label: a webhook from the Git server makes it immediate
rolling back is git revert: the same road, in reverse
people can keep read-only access to prod

lines.text: So here's a release now. Version 0.2.0 has been fine on go-dev, so someone opens a pull request that changes one line: the tag in the prod overlay.
lines.say: So here's a release now. Version zero point two point zero has been fine on go dev, so someone opens a pull request that changes one line: the tag in the prod overlay.

lines.text: A teammate reviews it, and then it's merged.
Argo CD checks the repository every two to three minutes, sees the new commit, and syncs.
The Deployment rolls out as usual, with the probes from Episode 6 deciding when each new pod gets traffic.
A webhook from the Git server can tell Argo CD the moment main moves, instead of waiting.
Rolling back is a git revert, which goes through the same review and the same sync.
And since nobody applies by hand anymore, people can have read-only access to prod.

steps.command: kubectl get deploy golinks -n golinks -o jsonpath='{..image}'; echo

lines.text: Here it is. The release commit is on main.
Within a couple of minutes, golinks goes out of sync: Git has a new tag, the cluster has the old one.
lines.say: Within a couple of minutes, go links goes out of sync: Git has a new tag, the cluster has the old one.

lines.text: Argo CD syncs. Health reads progressing while the new pods start and pass their probes, then healthy.
And the Deployment runs 0.2.0. Nobody touched the cluster.
lines.say: And the Deployment runs zero point two point zero. Nobody touched the cluster.

boxes.label: all of it kept in sync from Git, by Argo CD

lines.text: That's the whole road. A small k3s cluster, a real service with its database, and a name people can type.
lines.say: That's the whole road. A small K three S cluster, a real service with its database, and a name people can type.

lines.text: Health checks and logs, so you know when it's sick. Certificates from the company's own CA, and tokens from Keycloak.
Scaling with load, and a dev copy to try things in first.
And now all of it held in place from Git, by the same kind of loop we started with.

scenes.title: Thanks for watching
scenes.subtitle: Kubernetes, one go link at a time

lines.text: A last tip: Argo CD, cert-manager and the logging stack are still applied by hand. They can be Applications too, even Argo CD itself, so the whole cluster lives in Git.
Thanks for following along.
